The Power of Efficiency

When I first heard the term "efficiency" in the context of statistical computing, I thought it meant making code run faster—optimizing loops, reducing memory usage similar to what it was like in my CS classes. But through the class, I have come to understand that efficiency in data science is more about writing code that is easy to read, easy to modify, and easy to maintain. True efficiency isn't just about speed; rather about reducing the mental load on both the programmer and the reader, reducing opportunities for errors, and creating elegant solutions that can be gracefully scaled.

What is Efficiency in Statistical Computing?

In statistical computing, efficiency has multiple levels:

1. Computational Efficiency: Code that runs quickly and uses memory wisely. Using vectorized operations instead of loops, avoiding unnecessary copying of data similarly to standard programming.

2. Coding Efficiency: Writing less code to accomplish the same task. This reduces the chance of errors and makes the code easier to understand.

3. Cognitive Efficiency: Creating code that's easy to understand and modify aka reproducibility.

4. Maintenance Efficiency: Building solutions that are easy to update when requirements change.

What Does Efficiency Look Like?

Using functions instead of copy-paste:** When I first started coding, if I needed to do something three times, I would literally copy and paste code three times, changing the variable names each time. This is extremely inefficient —it's tedious to write, error-prone, and difficult to maintain.

In Lab 7, I learned to write a rescale_01() function instead. Rather than:

# Rescale length 
fish$length_scaled <- (fish$length - min(fish$length, na.rm = TRUE)) / 
                      (max(fish$length, na.rm = TRUE) - min(fish$length, na.rm = TRUE))

# Rescale weight 
fish$weight_scaled <- (fish$weight - min(fish$weight, na.rm = TRUE)) / 
                      (max(fish$weight, na.rm = TRUE) - min(fish$weight, na.rm = TRUE))

I could write once and use many times:

# efficient
rescale_01 <- function(x) {
  (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}

fish$length_scaled <- rescale_01(fish$length)
fish$weight_scaled <- rescale_01(fish$weight)

Using iteration instead of repetition: Instead of calling a function multiple times an even more efficient solution is using iteration to apply it systematically. In Lab 9, instead of:

# not efficient
class(surveys$record_id)
class(surveys$month)  
class(surveys$day)
class(surveys$year)
# ... repeat for 13 variables

I learned to write:

# efficient
map_chr(surveys, class)

Using across() for multiple columns: In Lab 9 Question 4, I needed to convert all character columns to factors. The inefficient approach would be:

# not efficient
evals$course_id <- as.factor(evals$course_id)
evals$weekday <- as.factor(evals$weekday)
evals$academic_degree <- as.factor(evals$academic_degree)
# ... repeat for each character column

Using map_if(), I could write:

# efficient
evals_new <- evals |>
  map_if(is.character, as.factor) |>  
  bind_cols()

What Does Efficiency Allow You to Do?

Tackle Problems at Scale: In Lab 10, where I ran 10,000 simulations, if I wasn't using efficient code like map_int(), the question would be practically impossible:

results <- map_int(.x = 1:10000, .f = ~ randomBabies(4))

Similarly, the confidence interval coverage simulation involved running 1,000 iterations of generating data, fitting models, and checking coverage. The efficient approach:

ci_dat <- map(.x = 1:1000, .f = ~mycifun(beta0 = 3, beta1 = 0.5, n = 100))
ci_results <- bind_rows(ci_dat)

Experiment and Iterate Quickly: In Lab 8, I wrote a style_plot() wrapper function that could apply different themes and color palettes to any ggplot object:

style_plot <- function(plot, theme_fn = theme_minimal, 
                       palette = NULL, aesthetic = "color") {
  # ... 
}

This efficient code allowed me to quickly try out different visual styles:

# Try different themes 
style_plot(my_plot, theme_fn = theme_bw)
style_plot(my_plot, theme_fn = theme_classic)
style_plot(my_plot, theme_fn = theme_minimal)

Without this code, I would have to rebuild the plot each time or copy-paste large chunks of code.

Build on Previous Work: In Lab 8 Question 1, I created a rescale_column() function that used my earlier rescale_01() function as a helper:

rescale_column <- function(data, cols) {
  data |> 
    mutate(across(.cols = {{ cols }}, .fns = rescale_01))
}

This is efficiency through composition— the idea of building complex things through small or easy building blocks/chunks. Each function does one thing, and when combined they create complex workflows.

Why is Efficiency Important?

1. Reduces Errors: Every line of code is an opportunity for a mistake. For example, in Challenge 7, my initial replace_outliers() function had a bug in one of three repeated sections. If I'd written it efficiently from the start, that bug would have been impossible—there would only be one section to get right.

2. Enables Professional Work: Real data science projects have tight deadlines and changing requirements. In my internship at Zencargo, I worked on workflow automation where requirements changed frequently. Efficient code—using functions, iteration, and abstraction—made it possible to adapt quickly.

3. Allows Focus on the Important Parts: The less time I spend on repetitive mechanics, the more time I can spend on the more interesting, complex parts. In Lab 10's coverage visualization, I could focus on making the statistical concept clear because I wasn't bogged down in repetitive plotting code.

Aha Moments About Efficiency

Aha Moment 1: Lab 7

When I first wrote the rescale_01() function in Lab 7, I thought "this seems like a lot of code for such a simple operation." But then in Lab 7 Question 7, I needed to create side-by-side histograms of original vs. rescaled data. Instead of recalculating the rescaling formula, I just called my function:

fish %>%
  mutate(length_scaled = rescale_01(length)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = length_scaled)) + 
  geom_histogram()

The function I'd written earlier saved me from potential errors and made Question 7 easier.

Aha Moment 2: Lab 9

In Lab 9, when I wrote map_chr(surveys, class) to get the data type of every variable, I had a big aha moment. Without map, I would have written 13 lines of code. But if the dataset had 100 variables or 1000 it would have taken me a lot of effort to write the code. This made me realize that efficiency is key to be able to scale code. The efficient solution works just as well for 10 variables as for 10,000, which is why it is important.

The Bigger Picture

The most important thing I've learned about efficiency is that it's not about saving time in the moment rather about creating code that is easy to read, replicate and reuse.

The principles of efficiency I learned in STAT 331—abstraction through functions, iteration instead of repetition, building composable tools—are principles I'll use throughout my career.
